title: Writing as Naomi Neville and who owns the Minit catalog
summary: He used his mother's maiden name during a contract dispute; Minit was sold to Imperial and publishing rights sit with Travis Music.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Why in the 60s did you write under the name Naomi Neville? Naomi Neville. Naomi.

That's my mother's maiden name. out in Tibidore and Shriburri pronounced it John Neville, which was my grandfather. I had, when mother-in-law was written and things before that, I was underage. And there were people that would come through town and collect a lot of things, masters, and they'd sell them out to different companies. And I was a product of that for a while. It's just not so terrible. It just was a way of doing things at that time. And I was out on a particular label, which was an alright label. But after that, there was no more affiliations actually, or things being done or even undone. And later, as I began to go into a business with others, it became a problem on whether that contract was still valid or void. So until they got that straight, I wrote under Naomi Neville. And it took a while, but for that period, I did write under Naomi Neville.
Who has all the old Minute material, like all the old tapes of that?

Minute was sold to Liberty Records. Not Liberty Act. Minute was sold to Imperial. That used to distribute Minute. Imperial, I think, was bought out by Liberty Records. Maybe Liberty was bought out by someone else. The company was Travis Music, a publishing company. And Post, that's how the statements would come. So they are the ones who actually have the legitimate titles to publish. And the songs. As far as tapes of a lot of those things, I probably have a seven and a half of a lot of them. They just got onto a stacking stadium in the comments.
